summary: Solid, multi-source core for a 7-10 sentence beginner story. Chaac (Chaak, Cháak) is the Maya god of rain, thunder and lightning, shown with a long drooping nose, fangs, scaly reptile-or-frog-like skin and a lightning axe; he strikes the clouds with the axe and thunder and rain come. There are four Chaacs tied to the directions and colours (east red, north white, west black, south yellow). In Yucatan villages farmers still hold the Ch'a' Cháak (Cha Chaac) rain ceremony, led by a h-men (Maya priest), at a square wooden altar with food and drink: balche (honey and tree-bark drink), maize bread (noj waj), sakab (honey maize drink), a thick broth (cho k'ob), and prayers in Maya. Four boys croak like frogs to call the rain. Farmers ask for rain because northern Yucatan has no surface rivers and the milpa (maize field) depends on the rainy season; drought means a poor harvest. The ceremony is now rarer than before and mixes Maya and Catholic elements.
facts: Chaac (also spelled Chaak, Cháak, Chac; Chaahk in Classic Maya) is the Maya god of rain, thunder and lightning, and a patron of farming and the maize harvest. [Wikipedia; Britannica; World History Encyclopedia via search; mayan.org]

Appearance: a human-like body with scaly reptile- or amphibian-like skin and a non-human head with fangs and a long, drooping (pendulous) nose; the long nose is his best-known identifier. In Classic-style art a shell is his ear ornament. Britannica adds large round eyes. [Wikipedia; Britannica; mayan.org]

He carries a lightning axe (often with a shield). With the axe he strikes the clouds, and that makes thunder and rain. The axe stands for the lightning bolt that splits the clouds. [Wikipedia; mayan.org]

Chaac is also four Chaacs, one for each direction, each with a colour: east red, north white, west black, south yellow (Wikipedia adds green for the centre). In 16th-century Yucatan the east one was called Chac Xib Chaac, 'Red Man Chaac'. No single colour for 'the' Chaac is attested; the colours belong to the four directional Chaacs. [Wikipedia; Britannica; mayan.org]

Chaac is linked to water sources: lesser Chaacs were believed to live in caves and cenotes (natural sinkholes) and refill their water. A modern h-men, Abelardo Tut Uicah, says 'Rain collects in cenotes, bringing life, so we pray to Cháak, who lives inside them.' [HistoricalMX; Mongabay 2024; Yucatan Today 2025]

The Ch'a' Cháak (also written Ch'a Chaak, Cha Chaak, Cha-Chaac, Ch'aa Chaac) is a Yucatec Maya agricultural ceremony to ask for rain and good harvests; it is still held in some villages (examples: Yaxcaba, Sotuta, Dzitas and Espita, Tzucacab, Hunucma). [Mongabay 2024; Por Esto 2020/2021/2023; Yucatan.com.mx 2025; Yucatan Living 2017]

The ceremony is led by a h-men (also written j-men, jmeen, h-meen): a Maya ritual specialist or priest. The h-men prays in Maya, chants, uses incense smoke, and gives the offerings to the Chaacs and other beings. Mongabay names working h-men in 2024 (Abelardo Tut Uicah, Idelfonso Yah Alcocer). [Mongabay 2024; Mexico Desconocido; Yucatan Today 2025; Yucatan.com.mx 2025]

Tut Uicah began training at age 13 under a priest from Peto; as a small boy of about seven he played the frog (sapo) role in the ceremony. Fewer young people now train to become h-men. [Yucatan Today 2025]

The altar is a square table or frame built from freshly cut wood and leaves from the forest/bush. It stands for the universe, and each side is a direction: xaman (north), nojol (south), lak'in (east), chik'in (west). Vines or posts mark the four corners. [Mexico Desconocido; Por Esto 2020/2021/2023; Mongabay 2024; mayan.org]

Offering drink 1: balche, a ritual drink made by fermenting the bark of the balche tree (Lonchocarpus violaceus) with honey and water. It is poured or splashed and shared; it is offered to the guardians and, at the end, to the people present. The h-men prepares it some days ahead. [Wikipedia Balche; Mexico Desconocido; Por Esto 2020/2021; HRAF/Yale via search]

Offering drink 2: sakab (sacab), a maize drink sweetened with honey, set in thirteen gourd cups (jicaras: twelve around and one in the centre). [Por Esto 2020/2021/2023; Yucatan Today 2025 (Sacab ritual)]

Offering food: maize bread/large tortillas. Noj wajes ('big breads') are thirteen-layer masa breads with ground squash seed (pepita) and beans; in Mexico Desconocido the breads are dough balls with ground squash seed wrapped in leaves. They are cooked or buried in the pib (underground earth oven) before being offered. Mongabay also shows maize dough cooked in a pib. [Por Esto 2020/2023; Mexico Desconocido; Mongabay 2024]

Offering food: cho k'ob (chok'ob), a thick broth/stew (made with k'ool, a thickened sauce) in which bread and meat are broken up; it is given first to the invoked guardians and then shared with the people. Chickens, turkeys and venison are also mentioned as the meat in different villages. [Mexico Desconocido; Por Esto 2020/2023; Riviera Maya News 2024; HistoricalMX]

Four boys, one at each corner of the altar, croak like frogs during the prayers to call the rain. This is described by Wikipedia, mayan.org, Yucatan Living, Por Esto 2021, and Yucatan Today (a h-men remembers playing the frog as a boy). [Wikipedia; mayan.org; Yucatan Living 2017; Por Esto 2020/2021; Yucatan Today 2025]
In one 2021 Dzitas ceremony the guardians also whistled, sounded a gourd and struck vines against a vessel of water to imitate falling rain. [Por Esto 2021]

Thunder: Chaac makes thunder by striking the clouds with his axe. In one reported ceremony (Mexico Desconocido), thunder was heard far away as it began, a drizzle followed after a long drought, and by the end the rain was steady and the frogs sang without stopping. [Wikipedia; Mexico Desconocido]

Why farmers ask for rain: northern Yucatan has almost no rivers or lakes on the surface, rain drains quickly into the limestone, and the maize milpa depends on the rains (roughly May to October). If rain is late or fails, the harvest is poor and water sources can dry up. In 2024 Yucatan had its worst drought in about 50 years and rains came over a month late. [mayan.org; Mongabay 2024; HRAF/Yale via search]

The ceremony asks for rain so crops can grow that year, and also says thank you for what the land has given; it is a community event with families preparing food together and sharing it afterwards. [Por Esto 2020/2021/2023; Yucatan.com.mx 2025]

The ceremony has become rarer: elders in Telchac Puerto said it has nearly vanished, and in 2024 drought revived it in some villages such as Yaxcaba. [Riviera Maya News 2024; Mongabay 2024; Yucatan.com.mx 2025]
variants: Name of the ceremony: Ch'a' Cháak, Ch'a Chaak, Cha Chaak, Cha-Chaac, Ch'aa Chaac. Literal gloss varies by source: 'rain calling' (Flores and Kantun Balam 1997, per secondary summary) and 'to bring Cháak' (travel guide). Use 'Ch'a' Cháak' with a simple gloss such as 'calling the rain'.

Who is asked: some sources address Chaak directly (Wikipedia, Mongabay); Por Esto and a cultural promoter from Espita say the rain is requested from the Yumtsilo'ob ('Lords/Creators'); Mexico Desconocido lists Chaac plus guardian spirits (yumbalames, aluxes) and Catholic saints. Core: villagers ask the rain deities, with Chaac the best-known one.
Name of the priest: h-men (most common in English), j-men/jmeen/J-meen (Spanish-Maya spelling), h-meen. Some newspaper reports just say 'sacerdote maya' (Maya priest).
Place: traditionally in the monte/milpa with few people (CICY, via search summary); today also in village yards, church grounds or open lots so more people can attend (Yucatan.com.mx 2025; Por Esto).

Timing: before planting (travel guide), around the start of the planting season (Yucatan Living), or during a drought (HistoricalMX; Mongabay). Duration varies: a day (many reports), two days (Telchac Puerto), three days (HistoricalMX), four to seven days (Flores and Balam 1997, per secondary summary). Avoid giving a fixed length.

Meat offerings differ by village: chickens (very common), turkey, duck, sheep, venison. Bread is called noj waj / noj wajes / pibes / panes; sizes and layers (13 layers in Espita/Dzitas, 42 small plus 4 large breads in Mexico Desconocido) vary.

Altar details differ: square table with arches and a hanging gourd (Mexico Desconocido), cross at the centre and corners with Bacabs (Espita/Dzitas), vines at the four corners (Mongabay). Core: a square, four-direction altar.

Colour of Chaac: only the four directional Chaacs have colours (red east, white north, black west, yellow south); one site (mayan.org) also mentions Maya blue and black paint in a codex-style caption. Do not fix one colour.

Frog boys: most sources say four boys at the corners; Por Esto 2020/2021 adds that their feet are tied with vine (only in this source), another says they sit under the altar (via a 1970s account, secondary summary). Use only 'four boys croak like frogs'.

maya_terms.meaning: the Maya god of rain, thunder and lightning; in Yucatec chaak also means rain; plural: the Chaaks (four, one per direction)

maya_terms.term: Ch'a' Cháak / Ch'a Chaak / Cha Chaak
maya_terms.meaning: the rain-asking ceremony; 'rain calling' or 'to bring Cháak'

cautions: Human sacrifice (young men or objects thrown into cenotes) is attached to Chaac in old accounts but is contested by modern analysis; leave it out of a family story.

Balche is a fermented, mildly alcoholic drink. For a beginner/children's story say only 'a sweet honey drink' or 'a special drink made with honey and bark', not alcohol, and do not say children drink it.
Animal offerings (chickens sacrificed with balche, hunted deer) can be upsetting; a story should say 'food is prepared and shared' rather than describe killing.

Religion: the modern ceremony blends Maya and Catholic elements (saints such as San Isidro; thirteen layers read as 12 apostles plus Jesus or 13 heavens; a cross on the altar). Interpretations are the village's own; avoid saying what the Maya 'believe' as a single fact, use 'the villagers say / the h-men prays'.

Do not claim the ceremony always makes it rain. One article reports rain following; the 11-of-12 figure from Flores and Balam 1997 came only from a secondary summary (PDF is scanned, could not be read), so do not quote it.
The thunder 'sound' is only attested as Chaac's axe striking the clouds; no source gives a Maya description of how it sounds (rumble, boom). Any sound word in the story is storytelling licence.
Colour of Chaac is not single: only the four directional Chaacs are red, white, black, yellow. Avoid 'Chaac is blue'; blue/green are not consistently sourced.

Single-source details to omit or hedge: 'feet tied with vine' (only Por Esto), 'uo' for frog (only mayan.org), 'x'men' as guardians (Riviera Maya News, unclear), and the 2024 Progreso Poseidon-statue episode (Wikipedia, news-level).

mayan.org, travel blogs and Yucatan Living are popular/secondary; the strongest sources here are Wikipedia/Britannica (general), Mongabay and Yucatan Today (named h-men, 2024-25), and Por Esto / Mexico Desconocido (village detail). The Flores and Balam 1997 and CICY PDFs could not be read, so facts attributed to them come from search summaries only; the Britannica page was reached through search results only (direct fetch returned 403).

The ceremony is declining and is a living religious practice; write respectfully, in the present tense for 'some villages still hold it', and avoid caricature (no 'primitive' or 'superstition' wording). Beware paid 'ceremonies' for tourists (Por Esto 2023 on charlatans); do not portray it as a tourist show.
The SEP 'Nuestra cosmovision' page that mentions CH'A'ACHAAK concerns Popoloca (Puebla) communities, not Yucatec; it was excluded.
